title: Grateful Dead Live at Fillmore West on 1970-06-04
source: Audience Recording by Gerry Olsen. Sony TC-124 single-capstan portable cassette deck equipped with Sony F-99S One Point Stereo Dynamic Microphone IMP LOW (hand-held). 120 minute BASF normal bias tape. Lineage via Dan McDonald (droncit@yahoo.com): Master Audience Cassette->Nakamichi BX-1 (modified for flat transfer)-> Tascam DR-07MK2 (24-bit, 96kHz); DC8Forensics was used to apply the NAB curve for normal bias cassettes. Converted to 16-bit, 44.1kHz using 32-bit interpolation and a triangular high pass dither. After the NAB curve in a multifilter I applied a virtual vale and overtone generator for lost harmonics and used a channel blender to blend below 150 Hz to mono to minimize mic handling noise.

ai_review.summary: Superior audience tape captures the three‑part acoustic → NRPS → electric June 4 1970 Fillmore West show, highlighted by a smoking St. Stephen > Midnight Hour > Not Fade Away sequence.
ai_review.review: The recording is an audience capture (with a brief soundboard excerpt for the first set) that sounds clear and upfront, though listeners often boost lows and highs with EQ to get the best balance. Musically the show shines – the acoustic set, the NRPS interlude, and especially the electric second set deliver classic moments like the St. Stephen > Midnight Hour > Not Fade Away segue and a thrilling China → Rider transition, all punctuated by Jerry’s pedal‑steel work and Mickey Hart’s distinctive drumming.

ai_rating.rationale: Average reviewer rating is ~4.33/5 across nine reviews, with consistent praise for both performance and tape quality; weighting favors the strong musical show.

recording_quality.technical_notes: Clear upfront sound praised by multiple listeners; some EQ adjustments recommended; first set includes a brief soundboard fragment, while NRPS and electric sets “sizzle” despite being audience‑only.

standout_songs: St. Stephen > Midnight Hour > Not Fade Away
show_quality.setlist_flow: The three‑part structure (acoustic, NRPS, electric) is lauded for its smooth transitions and historic 1970 vibe, with especially strong segues between St. Stephen and the jam and between China and Rider.

band_member_comments.Jerry: Pedal steel and guitar work repeatedly praised; described as sweet, perfect‑tone, and a key part of the show’s dynamics.
band_member_comments.Drums: Mickey Hart’s drumming noted as "decidedly non‑country country" on the NRPS set, adding character to the performance.
